subject: Physics
title: Rohan's Market Quest: Measuring the World
hook: A shopkeeper's scales, a surveyor's tape, and why the whole world agrees on how to measure.

slides.title: Units and Measurements
slides.storyContext: Rohan visits the local vegetable market with his teacher Mr. Sharma and discovers why measurement matters.

image.alt: Units and Measurements — Units and Measurements

slides.title: The Market Mystery
slides.storyContext: Rohan asks Anaya at the market: 'Why does your dad's scale show 1 kg, but the digital one shows 1000 grams?' Anaya's confused. Mr. Sharma steps in: 'Different units, same quantity. But here's the catch—if every shop used different units, chaos!' Rohan realizes: the whole world needs to agree on how to measure.

image.alt: The Market Mystery — Units and Measurements

slides.title: What is a Unit?
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma draws a line in the sand: 'A unit is a standard quantity we use to measure things.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: A unit is a standard quantity adopted by convention to measure a physical quantity.

points.label: Why?
points.text: Without units, '5' means nothing. 5 kg sugar ≠ 5 meters of rope ≠ 5 seconds of time.

points.label: Example
points.text: Length: meter (m), mass: kilogram (kg), time: second (s).

slides.inSimpleWords: A unit is like the answer to 'measuring what?' — it tells you if you're measuring kilos, meters, or seconds.

image.alt: What is a Unit? — Units and Measurements

slides.title: The SI Base Units (International Standard)
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma pulls out a reference card: 'In 1960, the world agreed on 7 fundamental units called SI base units. Every physical quantity is built from these 7.'

points.label: The 7 SI Base Units
points.text: Length (meter, m), Mass (kilogram, kg), Time (second, s), Current (ampere, A), Temperature (kelvin, K), Luminous intensity (candela, cd), Mole (mol).

points.label: Why SI?
points.text: Système International d'Unités — used by scientists worldwide. Ensures consistency.

points.label: Daily use in India
points.text: When you buy rice by kg, cook for minutes, measure cloth by meters—you are using SI.

slides.inSimpleWords: The whole world uses the same 7 building blocks to measure everything—like how all LEGO sets use the same-sized bricks.

image.alt: The SI Base Units (International Standard) — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Anaya's Confusion with the Scales
slides.storyContext: Anaya's father owns two scales: an old mechanical one and a new digital one. They show different numbers for the same tomato. Rohan and Anaya are baffled. Mr. Sharma grins: 'Not different numbers—different units! The old scale reads in 'ser' (an old Indian unit, about 900 g). The digital shows grams. It's the same tomato, just spoken in two languages.'

image.alt: Anaya's Confusion with the Scales — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Prefixes: Making Big and Small Numbers Easy
slides.storyContext: Rohan asks: 'Why do we say 1000 meters is 1 kilometer, not just 1000 meters?' Mr. Sharma smiles: 'Prefixes are shortcuts for big and small numbers.'

points.label: Large prefixes
points.text: kilo (k) = 10³, mega (M) = 10⁶, giga (G) = 10⁹, tera (T) = 10¹².

points.label: Small prefixes
points.text: milli (m) = 10⁻³, micro (μ) = 10⁻⁶, nano (n) = 10⁻⁹, pico (p) = 10⁻¹².

points.label: Real Indian examples
points.text: Your phone: gigabytes of data, nanoseconds to process. Monsoon rainfall: millimeters or centimeters. Distance to school: kilometers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Prefixes are labels that multiply the unit. 1 km = 1000 m (kilo means ×1000).

image.alt: Prefixes: Making Big and Small Numbers Easy — Units and Measurements

slides.title: The Land Surveyor's Challenge
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma mentions his weekend job: surveying land for a new school building. 'I measured 2500 meters. My colleague measured 2.5 kilometers. Same distance, different units. If we don't agree on units, we can't build the school straight!' Rohan nods: measurement errors destroy buildings.

image.alt: The Land Surveyor's Challenge — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Measurement Error & Significant Figures
slides.storyContext: Anaya's father measures sugar on an old scale (±50 g uncertainty) and a new digital scale (±1 g). Rohan asks: 'Which is correct?' Mr. Sharma: 'Both are, but one is more precise. And we only report as many digits as we can trust.'

points.label: Systematic error
points.text: The scale's zero mark is off—every reading is 10 g too high (always the same error).

points.label: Random error
points.text: The scale jiggles a bit—sometimes you read 100 g, sometimes 101 g.

points.label: Significant figures
points.text: Write only the digits you trust. If your scale reads ±1 g, write 250 g (3 sig figs), not 250.00 g (5 sig figs).

slides.inSimpleWords: Every measurement has tiny errors. Significant figures are the digits you can trust—don't pretend you're more precise than you really are.

image.alt: Measurement Error & Significant Figures — Units and Measurements

slides.title: The Gold Scam
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma tells a cautionary tale: 'A jeweler cheated a customer by using an inaccurate scale. The customer bought 10 grams of gold but received only 9.5 grams. Thousands of rupees lost! That's why measurement standards matter.' Rohan shivers: careless measurement ruins lives.

image.alt: The Gold Scam — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Dimensional Analysis & Unit Conversion
slides.storyContext: Rohan needs to convert the market's rice price from rupees per kilogram to rupees per gram. Mr. Sharma teaches him a trick: treat units like numbers in a fraction.

points.label: The trick
points.text: Multiply by a conversion factor = 1. E.g., 1 kg = 1000 g, so (1 kg)/(1000 g) = 1.

points.label: Example
points.text: 100 rupees/kg = 100 rupees/kg × (1 kg)/(1000 g) = 0.1 rupees/g.

points.label: Dimensional check
points.text: Always cancel units. If you end with wrong units (e.g., m/kg when you want m/s), you made an error.

slides.inSimpleWords: To convert units, multiply by a fraction that equals 1. The unwanted units cancel, and only the units you want remain.

image.alt: Dimensional Analysis & Unit Conversion — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Rules for Significant Figures (Detailed)
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma pulls out examples: '250 has 2 or 3 significant figures depending on context. 0.0035 has 2. Leading zeros don't count; trailing zeros do if there's a decimal point.'

points.label: Nonzero digits
points.text: Always significant. 456 has 3 sig figs.

points.label: Zeros between nonzero digits
points.text: Always significant. 402 has 3 sig figs.

points.label: Leading zeros
points.text: Never significant. 0.0042 has 2 sig figs (only 4 and 2).

points.label: Trailing zeros
points.text: Significant only if there's a decimal point. 50 has 1 sig fig; 50. has 2.

slides.inSimpleWords: Counting sig figs: include all digits except leading zeros. Trailing zeros count only if there's a decimal point.

image.alt: Rules for Significant Figures (Detailed) — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Worked Example: Density Calculation
slides.storyContext: Anaya's father wants to know the density of his cooking oil. He fills a 1-liter bottle (volume = 1000 cm³) and weighs it on the market scale: 920 g (not counting the bottle).

example.problem: Calculate the density of cooking oil in kg/m³. Given: mass = 920 g, volume = 1000 cm³.
example.solution: Step 1: Convert to SI units. Mass = 920 g = 0.92 kg; Volume = 1000 cm³ = 1000 × 10⁻⁶ m³ = 10⁻³ m³. Step 2: Density = mass/volume = 0.92 kg / 10⁻³ m³ = 920 kg/m³.

slides.inSimpleWords: Oil is lighter than water (which has density 1000 kg/m³), so oil floats—and our calculation confirms it: 920 < 1000.

image.alt: Worked Example: Density Calculation — Units and Measurements

slides.title: The Market Scales Showdown
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma organizes a test. He brings certified 1 kg weights and checks each shop's scale. Anaya's father's scale reads 1.02 kg (2% error). Another shop reads 0.97 kg (3% error). Mr. Sharma explains: 'Every tool has limits. We account for that with uncertainty.'

image.alt: The Market Scales Showdown — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Absolute & Relative Errors
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma teaches Rohan to quantify mistakes: 'Absolute error is the difference from the true value. Relative error tells you if the mistake is big or small compared to the true value.'

points.label: Absolute error
points.text: Δ = |measured value − true value|. E.g., if you measure 102 g but true is 100 g, Δ = 2 g.

points.label: Relative error
points.text: Δ/true value = 2/100 = 0.02 = 2%. Small and easy to compare.

points.label: Percentage error
points.text: Relative error × 100%. For the scale: 2% error. Anaya's father: 2%, another shop: 3%.

slides.inSimpleWords: Absolute error tells you how far off you are in actual units. Relative error tells you if that mistake is big or small for what you're measuring.

image.alt: Absolute & Relative Errors — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Old Units of India & History
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma adds: 'Before SI, India used many units. A 'gaj' is an old unit of length—about 1 meter. A 'maund' for weight. The British brought 'inches' and 'pounds.' Now we use meters and kilograms. Progress!'

points.label: Old units
points.text: Gaj (length), Ser (mass), Bigha (area), Danda (height measurement).

points.label: Impact on trade
points.text: Different regions used different units—trade was chaotic. SI unified everything.

points.label: Legacy
points.text: Some Indians still use old units in villages. Understanding them helps appreciate why standardization matters.

slides.inSimpleWords: India had many old units. SI replaced them so everyone—Indians and world—can trade and communicate without confusion.

image.alt: Old Units of India & History — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Your Turn: Convert Rainfall
slides.storyContext: During monsoon, Mr. Sharma tells Rohan: 'The forecast says 45 mm of rain will fall. If our roof is 10 m², how many liters of water will we collect?' (Hint: 1 m³ = 1000 L.)

example.problem: Calculate the volume of rainwater collected on a 10 m² roof with 45 mm of rainfall.
example.solution: Step 1: Convert depth to meters: 45 mm = 45 × 10⁻³ m = 0.045 m. Step 2: Volume = area × depth = 10 m² × 0.045 m = 0.45 m³. Step 3: Convert to liters: 0.45 m³ × 1000 L/m³ = 450 L.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rainfall depth × roof area = volume of water you can collect and store.

image.alt: Your Turn: Convert Rainfall — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Challenge: Find the Error in a Calculation
slides.storyContext: Rohan's friend calculated: 5 kg/m³ = 5 g/cm³. Mr. Sharma asks: 'Is that right? Check the units.'

example.problem: Verify: 5 kg/m³ = 5 g/cm³. Show the conversion step-by-step.
example.solution: 5 kg/m³ = 5 kg/m³ × (1000 g / 1 kg) × (1 m³ / 10⁶ cm³) = 5 × 1000 / 10⁶ g/cm³ = 5 × 10⁻³ g/cm³ = 0.005 g/cm³. NOT 5 g/cm³! The friend made an error.

slides.inSimpleWords: Always track units when converting. A small mistake in powers of 10 multiplies into a huge error.

image.alt: Challenge: Find the Error in a Calculation — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Propagation of Errors in Calculations
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma explains: 'If you add two measured quantities, their errors add. If you multiply, relative errors multiply.'

points.label: Adding/subtracting
points.text: A ± δA and B ± δB → (A + B) ± (δA + δB). Errors add.

points.label: Multiplying/dividing
points.text: Relative error of (A × B) = relative error of A + relative error of B.

points.label: Example
points.text: Length 5.0 ± 0.1 m, width 3.0 ± 0.1 m. Area = 15 m². Relative errors: 0.1/5 = 2%, 0.1/3 ≈ 3.3%. Combined: ~5.3%. Area = 15 ± 0.8 m².

slides.inSimpleWords: When you combine measurements, their uncertainties combine too. Multiplication is worse than addition.

image.alt: Propagation of Errors in Calculations — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Worked Example: Area with Uncertainty
slides.storyContext: Rohan measures a rectangular plot: length = 20.5 ± 0.5 m, width = 15.2 ± 0.3 m. What's the area with error bars?

example.problem: Calculate area and uncertainty: length 20.5 ± 0.5 m, width 15.2 ± 0.3 m.
example.solution: Area = 20.5 × 15.2 = 311.6 m². Relative error in length: 0.5/20.5 ≈ 2.44%. Relative error in width: 0.3/15.2 ≈ 1.97%. Combined relative error ≈ 4.41%. Absolute error in area ≈ 311.6 × 0.0441 ≈ 13.7 m². Final: 312 ± 14 m².

slides.inSimpleWords: Combined measurements have combined uncertainties. Always propagate errors through calculations.

image.alt: Worked Example: Area with Uncertainty — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Scientific Notation & Order of Magnitude
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma shows Rohan how scientists write huge and tiny numbers: 5 × 10¹² (5 trillion), 2.3 × 10⁻⁸ (0.000000023). 'This avoids confusion and makes comparisons easy.'

points.label: Order of magnitude
points.text: The power of 10 that roughly equals the number. 234,000 is order 10⁵ (roughly 100,000).

points.label: Indian context
points.text: India's population ~1.4 × 10⁹. Earth's radius ~6.4 × 10⁶ m. Electron mass ~9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg.

slides.inSimpleWords: Scientific notation puts big and small numbers in a standard form. Order of magnitude tells you the rough size.

image.alt: Scientific Notation & Order of Magnitude — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Challenge: Build Your Own Unit
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma asks: 'If Indians had designed a unit system, what base units would you choose? Temperature by cow milk (constant at 37°C), distance by monsoon rain (annual fall).' Rohan laughs: 'Impractical!' Mr. Sharma: 'Exactly why SI won—reproducible, universal, stable.'

example.problem: Why is the kilogram defined as the mass of a platinum cylinder, not something from nature (like 'mass of Earth')?
example.solution: Portability. A standard kilogram can be transported and compared directly to other scales. Earth's mass is hard to measure and changes. SI prioritizes consistency and accessibility over philosophical 'naturalness.''

slides.inSimpleWords: Units must be stable, portable, and reproducible worldwide. That's why we use standard objects, not natural phenomena.

image.alt: Challenge: Build Your Own Unit — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Derived Units & Dimensional Analysis Recap
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma summarizes: 'All physical quantities can be expressed in terms of the 7 base units. Even complex ones like force (Newton = kg⋅m/s²) are built from them.'

points.label: Common derived units
points.text: Speed (m/s), acceleration (m/s²), force (N = kg⋅m/s²), energy (J = kg⋅m²/s²).

points.label: Dimensional consistency
points.text: Any physical equation must have matching dimensions on both sides. E.g., distance = speed × time → [m] = [m/s] × [s] ✓.

points.label: Quick check
points.text: If your calculated answer has wrong units (e.g., m/s² when you expect m), you made an error.

slides.inSimpleWords: All units come from the 7 base units. Check dimensions to catch mistakes.

image.alt: Derived Units & Dimensional Analysis Recap — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Worked Example: Dimensional Analysis Problem
slides.storyContext: Rohan checks his friend's answer: 'I calculated force = mass × velocity. Is that right?' Using dimensional analysis: [N] vs [kg⋅(m/s)]. Doesn't match! Friend forgot acceleration. Correct: force = mass × acceleration.

example.problem: Check if F = m × v is dimensionally correct. (Hint: F has units of Newtons.)
example.solution: [Force] = kg⋅m/s². [m × v] = kg × (m/s) = kg⋅m/s. These don't match! The equation is wrong. Correct form: F = m × a → [kg] × [m/s²] = [kg⋅m/s²] ✓

slides.inSimpleWords: Dimensional analysis catches errors before you do calculations. Match units on both sides.

image.alt: Worked Example: Dimensional Analysis Problem — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Modern Measurement Tools & Technology
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma shows Rohan modern tools: laser distance meters (±2 mm), atomic clocks (±nanoseconds), and weighing machines with digital precision. 'Technology improves accuracy, but the SI units remain the reference.'

points.label: Laser measurement
points.text: Uses light to measure distance with millimeter precision. Based on SI meter.

points.label: Atomic time
points.text: Cesium clocks define the second by vibration frequency. ±nanosecond precision.

points.label: Digital scales
points.text: Load cells measure force precisely. Display weight in SI kilograms.

slides.inSimpleWords: Modern tech makes measurements more precise, but always references SI units as the standard.

image.alt: Modern Measurement Tools & Technology — Units and Measurements

slides.title: The Grand Finale: Rohan's Assignment
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma challenges Rohan to measure the market's perimeter. 'Use any method, but tell me the error bars and significant figures.' Rohan measures three times: 142.5 m, 142.8 m, 143.1 m. Average = 142.8 m. Uncertainty = 0.3 m. Final answer: 142.8 ± 0.3 m.

image.alt: The Grand Finale: Rohan's Assignment — Units and Measurements

slides.title: What You've Learned
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma summarizes as they leave the market: 'Measurement connects theory to reality. Without agreed units and careful technique, physics is just stories.'

points.text: A unit is a standard quantity for measuring physical quantities.
The 7 SI base units (meter, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, candela, mole) are the foundation.
Prefixes (kilo-, milli-, micro-, etc.) make large and small numbers easy to write.
Errors exist; significant figures show precision. Don't claim more accuracy than you have.
Dimensional analysis and unit conversion are the tools to get right answers.
Absolute error = measured − true; Relative error = absolute error / true value.
Always report: value ± uncertainty. E.g., 142.8 ± 0.3 m.

slides.inSimpleWords: Measurement is the language of physics. Learn the SI units, be honest about precision, and always check your units when converting.

image.alt: What You've Learned — Units and Measurements

subject: Physics
title: Priya's Delhi Metro Journey: Velocity, Acceleration, and Graphs
hook: A commute on the world's fastest metro reveals how to describe and predict motion mathematically.

slides.title: Motion in a Straight Line
slides.storyContext: Priya rides Delhi Metro from her home to her physics coaching. Coach Vikram sits beside her with a stopwatch, turning a simple commute into a physics lesson.

image.alt: Motion in a Straight Line — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: The Metro's Secret
slides.storyContext: As the metro accelerates smoothly from the station, Coach Vikram asks Priya: 'Feel that push in your back? That's acceleration. In 30 seconds, we go from 0 to 80 km/h. Can you predict our speed at 15 seconds?' Priya realizes: if she knows how velocity changes, she can predict the future.

image.alt: The Metro's Secret — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: Distance, Displacement & Speed, Velocity
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram explains: 'You walked to the metro station (400 m away), but if I ask your displacement, it's the straight-line distance from home to station—only 300 m, because the path wasn't straight.'

points.label: Distance
points.text: Total path length (always positive). You walked 400 m, so distance = 400 m.

points.label: Displacement
points.text: Straight-line change from start to finish, with direction. From home to station = 300 m North.

points.label: Speed
points.text: Scalar: distance/time. You covered 400 m in 5 minutes, so speed = 400/300 = 1.33 m/s.

points.label: Velocity
points.text: Vector: displacement/time. Displacement 300 m / 5 min = 1 m/s North.

slides.inSimpleWords: Distance is 'how far you traveled'; displacement is 'how far you ended up from where you started.' Speed doesn't care about direction; velocity does.

image.alt: Distance, Displacement & Speed, Velocity — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: The Stopwatch Experiment
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram starts his stopwatch as the metro leaves the station. Every 5 seconds, he marks the position: 0 s → 0 m, 5 s → 12 m, 10 s → 25 m, 15 s → 37 m, 20 s → 50 m. 'Notice the pattern?' Priya calculates: 'The gaps increase—12, 13, 12, 13, 12 meters. We're accelerating!'

image.alt: The Stopwatch Experiment — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: Acceleration: The Rate of Change of Velocity
slides.storyContext: The metro leaves the station. At 0 s, speed = 0 m/s. At 10 s, speed = 5 m/s. At 20 s, speed = 10 m/s. Coach Vikram asks: 'What's the pattern?'

points.label: Definition
points.text: Acceleration a = Δv / Δt (change in velocity divided by time taken).

points.label: For the metro
points.text: In the first 20 seconds, velocity changed by 10 m/s, so a = 10/20 = 0.5 m/s².

points.label: Direction matters
points.text: If speed increases, acceleration is positive (same direction as motion). If speed decreases (braking), acceleration is negative (opposite to motion).

slides.inSimpleWords: Acceleration tells you how fast your speed is changing. A car speeding up or slowing down is accelerating.

image.alt: Acceleration: The Rate of Change of Velocity — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: The Braking Test
slides.storyContext: At Rajiv Chowk station, the metro suddenly brakes. Coach Vikram announces: 'Now we're decelerating—acceleration in the opposite direction!' Priya and other passengers lurch forward. Coach explains: 'Negative acceleration, but still acceleration. A = −0.8 m/s².'

image.alt: The Braking Test — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: Kinematic Equations for Constant Acceleration
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram pulls out a notebook: 'If acceleration is constant (like the metro's smooth start), we can use three magic formulas to find distance, velocity, or time—even without a stopwatch.'

points.label: Equation 1
points.text: v = u + at (final velocity = initial velocity + acceleration × time)

points.label: Equation 2
points.text: s = ut + ½at² (distance = initial velocity × time + ½ × acceleration × time²)

points.label: Equation 3
points.text: v² = u² + 2as (final velocity² = initial velocity² + 2 × acceleration × distance)

points.label: Symbols
points.text: u = initial velocity, v = final velocity, a = acceleration, t = time, s = distance.

slides.inSimpleWords: These three equations connect velocity, acceleration, distance, and time. Pick which ones you know, and solve for what you want.

image.alt: Kinematic Equations for Constant Acceleration — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: Priya Solves the Prediction Problem
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram asks Priya to predict: 'The metro starts at 0 m/s and accelerates at 0.5 m/s² for 20 seconds. How fast are we going, and how far have we traveled?' Priya uses v = u + at: v = 0 + 0.5(20) = 10 m/s. Then s = ut + ½at²: s = 0 + ½(0.5)(400) = 100 m. Coach nods approvingly: 'Exactly!'

image.alt: Priya Solves the Prediction Problem — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: Position-Time & Velocity-Time Graphs
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram draws two graphs on his notebook. The first shows the metro's position over time (curved, because acceleration). The second shows velocity over time (a straight line, because constant acceleration).

points.label: s-t graph (position vs time)
points.text: Slope = velocity. Curved graph = acceleration changing. Straight line = constant velocity.

points.label: v-t graph (velocity vs time)
points.text: Slope = acceleration. Area under the curve = displacement. Straight line = constant acceleration.

points.label: For the metro
points.text: v-t graph starts at (0, 0), rises in a straight line to (20 s, 10 m/s). Slope = 0.5 m/s². Area = ½ × 20 × 10 = 100 m traveled.

slides.inSimpleWords: Graphs are shortcuts to see the story of motion. Position graph's slope = velocity. Velocity graph's slope = acceleration; area = distance.

image.alt: Position-Time & Velocity-Time Graphs — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: The Graph Master
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram sketches a complex v-t graph: constant velocity (flat line), then acceleration (rising line), then deceleration (falling line). 'This is every metro ride: smooth start, constant speed, smooth stop. Look at the graph and you see the entire journey without numbers.'

image.alt: The Graph Master — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: Free Fall: Motion Under Gravity Alone
slides.storyContext: At a tunnel entrance, a tunnel worker drops a tool. Coach Vikram: 'On Earth, gravity gives every object the same acceleration downward: g = 9.8 m/s². That's free fall. Air resistance doesn't exist in our ideal world—yet.'

points.label: Acceleration due to gravity
points.text: g = 9.8 m/s² (≈ 10 m/s² in quick math). Direction: downward (toward Earth's center).

points.label: Free fall equations
points.text: Same as kinematic equations, but a is always g (or −g if up is positive). h = ½gt² for distance fallen from rest.

points.label: Example: 1-second rule
points.text: Drop a ball from rest. At t = 1 s, distance fallen = ½ × 10 × 1² = 5 m. At t = 2 s, distance = ½ × 10 × 4 = 20 m.

slides.inSimpleWords: In free fall, acceleration is always 9.8 m/s² downward. Heavier and lighter objects fall at the same rate (in a vacuum).

image.alt: Free Fall: Motion Under Gravity Alone — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: The Dropped Phone Story
slides.storyContext: A passenger drops their phone on the metro platform. It falls from 1 meter high. Coach Vikram asks Priya: 'How long until it hits the ground?' She uses h = ½gt²: 1 = ½(10)t² → t = √0.2 ≈ 0.45 seconds. 'Less than half a second!'

image.alt: The Dropped Phone Story — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: Worked Example: Metro Acceleration
slides.storyContext: The metro starts from rest and accelerates at 0.5 m/s² for 20 seconds, then moves at constant velocity. Priya asks: 'How far did we travel during acceleration?'

example.problem: A metro train starts from rest (u = 0) and accelerates at a = 0.5 m/s² for t = 20 seconds. Find (1) final velocity and (2) distance traveled.

slides.inSimpleWords: In 20 seconds, the metro reaches 10 m/s and covers 100 meters—that's the length of the platform!

image.alt: Worked Example: Metro Acceleration — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: Average vs Instantaneous Velocity
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram clarifies: 'When you say the metro's average speed is 20 m/s, that's distance/time. But at any instant—say, 10 seconds into acceleration—the velocity is exactly v = u + at = 0 + 0.5(10) = 5 m/s. Different things!'

points.label: Average velocity
points.text: Total displacement / total time. E.g., 100 m / 20 s = 5 m/s.

points.label: Instantaneous velocity
points.text: Velocity at a specific moment. Read from v-t graph or calculate using v = u + at.

points.label: Connection
points.text: For constant acceleration, average velocity = (u + v) / 2 = (0 + 10) / 2 = 5 m/s.

slides.inSimpleWords: Average velocity is the overall trip speed. Instantaneous velocity is your speedometer reading right now.

image.alt: Average vs Instantaneous Velocity — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: Your Turn: Braking Problem
slides.storyContext: The metro approaches Rajiv Chowk station traveling at 15 m/s. The driver applies brakes with a deceleration of −2.5 m/s². Priya asks: 'How long until we stop, and how far does the train travel while braking?'

example.problem: A train moving at u = 15 m/s applies brakes (a = −2.5 m/s²). Find time to stop and distance during braking.
example.solution: Using v = u + at (final velocity v = 0): 0 = 15 + (−2.5)t → t = 6 seconds. Using s = ut + ½at²: s = 15(6) + ½(−2.5)(36) = 90 − 45 = 45 m.

slides.inSimpleWords: The train brakes for 6 seconds and travels 45 meters—almost the length of a cricket pitch!

image.alt: Your Turn: Braking Problem — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: Motion Equations & Graphical Interpretation
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram sketches the v-t graph and asks: 'The area under the curve is displacement. The slope is acceleration. Can you see why?'

points.label: Area under v-t curve
points.text: For constant acceleration, v-t is a triangle (if starting from rest). Area = ½ × base × height = ½ × t × v = ½t(u + at) = ut + ½at² = s. Area = displacement!

points.label: Slope of v-t
points.text: Slope = Δv / Δt = acceleration. Steep line = large acceleration. Flat line = zero acceleration.

points.label: For the metro
points.text: A 20-second ramp from 0 to 10 m/s has slope 0.5 m/s² and area 100 m.

slides.inSimpleWords: On a velocity-time graph, the slope tells you acceleration, and the area tells you distance traveled.

image.alt: Motion Equations & Graphical Interpretation — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: The Non-Constant Acceleration Problem
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram adds: 'Real metros don't accelerate uniformly. Early on, they accelerate hard (high a). As speed increases, they ease off (lower a). The v-t graph is curved, not straight. For now, we assume constant a—a simplification that works for short intervals.'

image.alt: The Non-Constant Acceleration Problem — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: Calculus Behind Kinematics (Optional Deep Dive)
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram hints: 'Mathematicians use calculus: acceleration = dv/dt (derivative of velocity). Velocity = ds/dt (derivative of position). The kinematic equations are solutions to these differential equations.'

points.label: Derivative connection
points.text: a = dv/dt. If a is constant, integrating gives v = u + at.

points.label: Integration
points.text: Integrating v = u + at with respect to time gives s = ut + ½at².

points.label: Why it matters
points.text: For non-constant acceleration, calculus is necessary. But for this course, constant-a cases use our three equations.

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivatives and integrals are the deep math behind motion. We use shortcuts (kinematic equations) for constant acceleration.

image.alt: Calculus Behind Kinematics (Optional Deep Dive) — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: Worked Example: Multi-Phase Motion
slides.storyContext: Priya's metro journey has three phases: (1) Accelerate 0 to 10 m/s in 20 s, (2) Coast at 10 m/s for 60 s, (3) Brake from 10 m/s to 0 in 15 s. Find total distance.

example.problem: Phase 1: u=0, a=0.5 m/s², t=20s. Phase 2: u=10, a=0, t=60s. Phase 3: u=10, a=−2/3 m/s², t=15s. Find total distance.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real journeys have multiple phases. Solve each phase separately, then add distances.

image.alt: Worked Example: Multi-Phase Motion — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: Challenge: Find Final Velocity Without Time
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram poses a tricky problem: 'The metro travels 200 m while accelerating at 0.5 m/s² from rest. What's the final velocity?' (Hint: use v² = u² + 2as, which doesn't need time.)

example.problem: A train starts from rest and accelerates at 0.5 m/s² over 200 m. Find final velocity without using time.

slides.inSimpleWords: The third kinematic equation (v² = u² + 2as) is a shortcut when you don't know time but know distance, acceleration, and initial velocity.

image.alt: Challenge: Find Final Velocity Without Time — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: Negative Acceleration & Direction Conventions
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram clarifies: 'Negative acceleration doesn't always mean 'slowing down.' If you're moving backward (negative direction) and accelerating backward (negative a), you're speeding up backward. Convention matters.'

points.label: Choose a direction
points.text: Define positive (e.g., forward). Then velocity and acceleration can be positive or negative.

points.label: Negative v, positive a
points.text: Moving backward but decelerating (slowing down). Example: car in reverse, braking.

points.label: Negative v, negative a
points.text: Moving backward and accelerating backward (speeding up). Example: car in reverse, gas pedal down.

slides.inSimpleWords: Signs matter. Negative acceleration can mean slowing down OR speeding up in reverse, depending on velocity's sign.

image.alt: Negative Acceleration & Direction Conventions — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: Challenge: Mixed Sign Problem
slides.storyContext: A metro is moving at −5 m/s (backward). Acceleration is +0.2 m/s². Is it speeding up or slowing down?

example.problem: Determine if velocity becomes more negative or less negative. Initial v = −5 m/s, a = +0.2 m/s², t = 10 s. Final v = ?
example.solution: v = u + at = −5 + 0.2(10) = −5 + 2 = −3 m/s. From −5 to −3: magnitude decreased. The metro is slowing down (moving backward but decelerating).

slides.inSimpleWords: When signs differ between v and a, the object is slowing down. When they match, it's speeding up.

image.alt: Challenge: Mixed Sign Problem — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: Jerk: The Rate of Change of Acceleration
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram adds an advanced idea: 'Acceleration changes over time in real life. The metro doesn't jump from 0 to 0.5 m/s² instantly—it ramps up. The rate of change of acceleration is called 'jerk.''

points.label: Definition
points.text: Jerk j = da/dt. Units: m/s³.

points.label: Passenger comfort
points.text: High jerk causes passengers to feel a sudden lurch. Smooth acceleration has low jerk.

points.label: Real vs ideal
points.text: Our kinematic equations assume constant a (zero jerk). Reality has jerk; that's an advanced topic.

slides.inSimpleWords: Jerk is how quickly acceleration changes. Smooth rides have low jerk; jerky rides have high jerk.

image.alt: Jerk: The Rate of Change of Acceleration — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: Worked Example: Combining Multiple Unknowns
slides.storyContext: Priya encounters a hard problem: 'A car accelerates from 10 m/s to 20 m/s and travels 300 m. Find acceleration and time separately.'

example.problem: Initial u = 10 m/s, final v = 20 m/s, distance s = 300 m. Find a and t.
example.solution: Step 1: Use v² = u² + 2as to find a: (20)² = (10)² + 2a(300) → 400 = 100 + 600a → a = 0.5 m/s². Step 2: Use v = u + at to find t: 20 = 10 + 0.5t → t = 20 s.

slides.inSimpleWords: When you have 3 unknowns, pick two kinematic equations to solve for the missing quantities.

image.alt: Worked Example: Combining Multiple Unknowns — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: Challenge: Stopping Distance (Real-World Safety)
slides.storyContext: Coach Vikram asks: 'A car brakes at −8 m/s² from 30 m/s (highway speed). How far does it travel before stopping?' This is critical for road safety design.

example.problem: Car at u = 30 m/s, a = −8 m/s², v = 0. Find stopping distance s.
example.solution: Using v² = u² + 2as: 0 = (30)² + 2(−8)s → 0 = 900 − 16s → s = 56.25 m. The car needs ~56 meters to stop.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stopping distance grows with the square of speed. Double speed → quadruple stopping distance!

image.alt: Challenge: Stopping Distance (Real-World Safety) — Motion in a Straight Line

slides.title: What You've Learned
slides.storyContext: As Priya steps off at her coaching center, Coach Vikram reminds her: 'Motion isn't random—it follows rules. Velocity, acceleration, and the kinematic equations tie them together.'

points.text: Displacement is a vector (with direction); distance is a scalar.
Velocity = displacement/time; speed = distance/time. Velocity is a vector.
Acceleration = change in velocity / time. It can be positive (speeding up) or negative (slowing down).
Three kinematic equations describe motion with constant acceleration: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as.
Graphs (s-t and v-t) show motion visually. Slope and area have physical meaning.
Free fall: g = 9.8 m/s² acts on all objects equally.
Average velocity = total displacement / total time; instantaneous velocity is the speed at an exact moment.

slides.inSimpleWords: Motion is predictable when acceleration is constant. Learn the equations, draw the graphs, and you can forecast where and when.

image.alt: What You've Learned — Motion in a Straight Line

subject: Physics
title: Arjun's Cricket Shot: Projectile Motion in 2D
hook: A cricket ball soars in an arc, and math explains why—vectors, components, and the beauty of parabolas.

slides.title: Motion in a Plane
slides.storyContext: At the cricket ground, Arjun hits a six. Coach Deepak asks: 'Can you predict where the ball lands?' The answer lies in 2D motion.

image.alt: Motion in a Plane — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: The Cricket Ball's Secret
slides.storyContext: Arjun's hit launches the ball at 20 m/s at 45° to the horizontal. Coach Deepak stops him: 'Before you celebrate, let's break that into two parts: horizontal motion (constant velocity) and vertical motion (free fall under gravity). Together, they make a parabola.'

image.alt: The Cricket Ball's Secret — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: Vectors & Components: Breaking Motion into Parts
slides.storyContext: Coach Deepak draws a right triangle: 'The ball's initial velocity (20 m/s at 45°) has two components: horizontal and vertical. Each acts independently.'

points.label: Component breakdown
points.text: For velocity v at angle θ: horizontal component vₓ = v cos(θ); vertical component vᵧ = v sin(θ).

points.label: Independence principle
points.text: Horizontal motion is unaffected by gravity. Vertical motion follows free-fall rules independently.

slides.inSimpleWords: A diagonal velocity can be split into horizontal (left-right) and vertical (up-down) parts. They don't interfere with each other.

image.alt: Vectors & Components: Breaking Motion into Parts — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: The Rise and Fall
slides.storyContext: Coach Deepak narrates Arjun's shot: 'At launch, the ball shoots up at 14.14 m/s and forward at 14.14 m/s. Gravity pulls down constantly—the upward speed decreases. At the peak (about 1 second), upward speed = 0. Then it falls, gaining downward speed. Meanwhile, horizontal speed never changes—14.14 m/s the whole flight.'

image.alt: The Rise and Fall — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: Projectile Motion: The Two-Axis Approach
slides.storyContext: Coach Deepak pulls out a whiteboard: 'Treat horizontal and vertical motion separately, using the equations you know from straight-line motion.'

points.label: Horizontal (x-direction)
points.text: No gravity here. Acceleration aₓ = 0. Velocity vₓ is constant. Distance x = vₓ × t.

points.label: Vertical (y-direction)
points.text: Gravity acts. Acceleration aᵧ = −g = −9.8 m/s². Use kinematic equations: vᵧ = vᵧ₀ − gt; y = vᵧ₀t − ½gt².

points.label: Combined motion
points.text: At time t, the ball is at (x, y) = (vₓt, vᵧ₀t − ½gt²). This gives a parabolic path.

slides.inSimpleWords: Horizontal motion is simple: distance = speed × time. Vertical motion is free fall (gravity pulls down). Both happen at the same time.

image.alt: Projectile Motion: The Two-Axis Approach — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: Zara's Fielding Prediction
slides.storyContext: Zara stands at field boundary, unsure where the ball will land. Coach Deepak challenges her: 'Use the kinematic equations. At what time will the ball return to ground level (y = 0)?' Zara solves: 0 = 14.14t − ½(10)t² → t(14.14 − 5t) = 0 → t = 0 or t = 2.83 s. She sprints, knowing the ball will land in 2.83 seconds.'

image.alt: Zara's Fielding Prediction — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: Range & Maximum Height
slides.storyContext: Zara (fielding) stands far away. Coach asks: 'Where will Arjun's ball land? And at what point is it highest?' He derives two formulas.

points.label: Maximum height H
points.text: The ball reaches maximum height when vᵧ = 0. Using vᵧ = vᵧ₀ − gt: t_max = vᵧ₀/g. Then H = vᵧ₀²/(2g).

points.label: For Arjun's shot
points.text: vᵧ₀ = 14.14 m/s. H = (14.14)² / (2 × 9.8) = 200/19.6 ≈ 10.2 m. The ball reaches 10 meters high!

points.label: Range R
points.text: Total time of flight: ball returns when y = 0, so t_total = 2vᵧ₀/g. Range R = vₓ × t_total = (v²/g) sin(2θ).

points.label: For 45° angle
points.text: R = (20²/9.8) sin(90°) = 400/9.8 ≈ 40.8 m. The ball lands about 41 meters away—a huge six!

slides.inSimpleWords: The highest point is where upward velocity becomes zero. Range is how far it travels before hitting the ground.

image.alt: Range & Maximum Height — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: Time of Flight & Trajectory Equation
slides.storyContext: Coach Deepak asks: 'How long is the ball in the air? And can we write y as a function of x (the ball's path)?'

points.label: Time of flight
points.text: The ball leaves the ground (y = 0) and returns at y = 0. Solving 0 = vᵧ₀t − ½gt²: t = 0 (start) or t = 2vᵧ₀/g (landing).

points.label: For Arjun's shot
points.text: t = 2 × 14.14 / 9.8 ≈ 2.89 seconds. The ball is in the air for nearly 3 seconds.

points.label: Trajectory equation
points.text: Eliminating t from x = vₓt and y = vᵧ₀t − ½gt²: y = x tan(θ) − [gx²/(2v² cos²θ)]. A parabola!

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: The ball rises (tan term dominates), then falls (−gx²/... term dominates). A perfect arc.

slides.inSimpleWords: The ball stays airborne for 2-3 seconds and traces a parabola—up, then down. The math describes the arc perfectly.

image.alt: Time of Flight & Trajectory Equation — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: The Magic Angle
slides.storyContext: Coach Deepak reveals: 'For maximum range, the launch angle must be exactly 45°. At any other angle—30° or 60°—the range is shorter. But interestingly, 30° and 60° give the same range! They complement each other.'

image.alt: The Magic Angle — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: Optimal Launch Angle for Different Scenarios
slides.storyContext: Coach Deepak extends the lesson: 'For maximum range on flat ground, 45° is optimal. But if you're shooting from a height (like hitting off a cliff), the optimal angle is less than 45°.'

points.label: On flat ground
points.text: Optimal angle = 45°. All launch speeds give maximum range at 45°.

points.label: From elevated position
points.text: Optimal angle < 45°. The higher you start, the shallower the angle.

points.label: For given range
points.text: Two angles work: θ and (90° − θ). E.g., 30° and 60° both achieve the same range (if speeds are adjusted).

slides.inSimpleWords: Launch angle matters. On flat ground, 45° is best. From higher ground, shoot shallower. Two different angles can hit the same target.

image.alt: Optimal Launch Angle for Different Scenarios — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: Relative Motion: The Fielder's Perspective
slides.storyContext: Zara is running after the ball. Coach Deepak asks: 'From Zara's moving viewpoint, the ball looks different than from the stand.'

points.label: Relative velocity
points.text: If Zara runs at vz = 5 m/s and the ball moves at vb = 14.14 m/s (horizontal), relative velocity = vb − vz = 9.14 m/s.

points.label: Why it matters
points.text: To catch the ball, Zara sees it moving at relative velocity, not ground velocity. Misjudging means a missed catch.

points.label: 3D extension
points.text: In real cricket, the ball also rotates (spin), changing air resistance. 2D analysis is the foundation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Motion looks different depending on who's watching. A fielder running toward the ball sees it approaching faster than a spectator does.

image.alt: Relative Motion: The Fielder's Perspective — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: Worked Example: The Six
slides.storyContext: Arjun launches the ball at 25 m/s at 30° to the horizontal. Find maximum height, range, and time of flight.

example.problem: A cricket ball is hit at initial velocity v = 25 m/s, angle θ = 30°. Find (1) maximum height, (2) range, and (3) time of flight.

slides.inSimpleWords: A 30° launch angle gives a 55-meter range and about 8 meters height—a powerful six down the ground!

image.alt: Worked Example: The Six — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: The Stadium Surprise
slides.storyContext: The cricket match is at a stadium with a boundary 60 m away. Arjun launches at 20 m/s at 45°. Coach Deepak calculates: range = 400/9.8 ≈ 40.8 m. 'The ball lands short! But if he hits at 22 m/s at the same angle—watch!' Range = 484/9.8 ≈ 49.4 m. Still short. At 25 m/s, range ≈ 63.8 m. 'That's a six—and beyond!'

image.alt: The Stadium Surprise — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: Your Turn: The Over-the-Head Catch
slides.storyContext: A batsman hits at 20 m/s at 30°. Zara stands 30 m away and can jump to 2.5 m height. Can she catch it mid-air? Find the ball's height at x = 30 m.

example.problem: A ball is launched at v = 20 m/s, θ = 30°. Find its height at horizontal distance x = 30 m.
example.solution: vₓ = 20 cos(30°) ≈ 17.32 m/s. vᵧ₀ = 20 sin(30°) = 10 m/s. Time to reach x = 30 m: t = 30 / 17.32 ≈ 1.73 s. Height: y = 10(1.73) − ½(10)(1.73)² = 17.3 − 15.0 ≈ 2.3 m. Zara can't catch it—just out of reach!

slides.inSimpleWords: By calculating the ball's position at a specific horizontal distance, you can predict if a catch is possible.

image.alt: Your Turn: The Over-the-Head Catch — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: Air Resistance & Real-World Projectiles
slides.storyContext: Coach Deepak notes: 'Our math ignores air resistance. In reality, a cricket ball slows down as it flies, reducing range by 10-20%. For now, assume ideal conditions—but real cricket has air friction, spin, and wind.'

points.label: Air drag
points.text: Slows the projectile proportional to velocity squared. Heavier objects (like cricket balls) are less affected than light ones (like ping-pong).

points.label: Magnus effect (spin)
points.text: A spinning cricket ball curves due to air vortices. Fast bowlers exploit this; our 2D math ignores it.

points.label: Why we start simple
points.text: Master the ideal case first. Real projectiles add layers of complexity.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real cricket balls don't follow perfect parabolas due to air, spin, and wind. Our math is a starting point.

image.alt: Air Resistance & Real-World Projectiles — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: The Wind Effect
slides.storyContext: A monsoon gust blows sideways at 3 m/s. Coach Deepak asks: 'How does this change Arjun's six?' Zara calculates: the ball's vertical and forward motion are unchanged, but sideways velocity adds 3 m/s. The range isn't affected (still 40.8 m), but the landing spot shifts perpendicular to the field!'

image.alt: The Wind Effect — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: Projectile Motion at Different Elevations
slides.storyContext: Coach Deepak poses: 'What if we hit from a platform 5 meters high instead of ground level?'

points.label: Extra time in air
points.text: Starting from y = 5 m: −5 = vᵧ₀t − ½gt². Takes longer to return than from ground level.

points.label: Increased range
points.text: More time in air → horizontal distance increases even if initial angle and speed are the same.

points.label: Optimal angle shifts
points.text: From elevation, the optimal launch angle for maximum range is < 45° (shallower).

slides.inSimpleWords: Launch from higher ground, and the ball travels farther because it has more time to fall.

image.alt: Projectile Motion at Different Elevations — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: Worked Example: Elevated Launch
slides.storyContext: Arjun stands on a 2-meter platform and hits at 20 m/s at 45°. Find range and time of flight.

example.problem: Launch from y₀ = 2 m at v = 20 m/s, θ = 45°. Find range and time of flight.
example.solution: vₓ = 14.14 m/s, vᵧ₀ = 14.14 m/s. Time of flight: 2 = 14.14t − ½(10)t² → 5t² − 14.14t − 2 = 0 → t ≈ 3.09 s. Range = 14.14 × 3.09 ≈ 43.7 m. (Compare: ground level gives 40.8 m.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Higher launch point means longer flight time and greater range, even at the same angle and speed.

image.alt: Worked Example: Elevated Launch — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: Parametric Equations & Elimination
slides.storyContext: Coach Deepak shows: 'We have two parametric equations: x(t) and y(t), both in terms of time. To find the trajectory y(x), we eliminate t.'

points.label: Parametric form
points.text: x = vₓt, y = vᵧ₀t − ½gt². Time t is the parameter.

points.label: Eliminate t
points.text: From x = vₓt, solve for t: t = x/vₓ. Substitute into y equation: y = vᵧ₀(x/vₓ) − ½g(x/vₓ)².

points.label: Result
points.text: y = (vᵧ₀/vₓ)x − (g/(2vₓ²))x² = x tan(θ) − (g/(2v₀² cos²(θ)))x². Parabola!

slides.inSimpleWords: By eliminating time, we transform two parametric equations into one Cartesian equation for the ball's path.

image.alt: Parametric Equations & Elimination — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: Challenge: Circular Motion (Bonus)
slides.storyContext: Coach Deepak extends the idea: 'Projectile motion is half of circular motion. In uniform circular motion, acceleration is constant (toward center) but velocity is always tangential. Can you describe it?'

example.problem: A ball moves in a circle of radius r = 2 m at speed v = 6 m/s. Find centripetal acceleration and period.
example.solution: Centripetal acceleration a_c = v²/r = (6)²/2 = 18 m/s² (toward center). Period T = 2πr/v = 2π(2)/6 ≈ 2.09 seconds (time for one full lap).

slides.inSimpleWords: In circular motion, the ball's direction changes constantly, so there's always acceleration pointing toward the center—even though speed is constant.

image.alt: Your Turn: Circular Motion (Bonus) — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: Symmetry in Projectile Motion
slides.storyContext: Coach Deepak reveals: 'Projectile motion is symmetric about the peak. Time to rise = time to fall. Speed at 1 meter height going up = speed at 1 meter height coming down (but opposite direction).'

points.label: Time symmetry
points.text: t_rise = t_fall = (total flight time) / 2.

points.label: Speed symmetry
points.text: At height h: speed up = speed down. Only direction differs (up vs down).

points.label: Energy view
points.text: Kinetic energy at launch = kinetic energy at landing (same height). Gravity's work cancels.

slides.inSimpleWords: Projectiles are symmetric. The upward journey mirrors the downward journey.

image.alt: Symmetry in Projectile Motion — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: The Reverse Problem: Predicting Launch from Impact
slides.storyContext: Zara sees where the ball lands: 42 m away, 2.5 seconds after launch. Coach Deepak asks: 'Can we work backward to find launch velocity and angle?' She sets up equations and solves—a detective-like reverse analysis of projectile motion.

image.alt: The Reverse Problem: Predicting Launch from Impact — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: Energy Perspective on Projectiles
slides.storyContext: Coach Deepak hints: 'Mechanics has two languages: forces (Newton) and energy (Joules). Both describe the same cricket shot, just differently.'

points.label: Kinetic energy
points.text: KE = ½mv². At launch, all KE. At peak, part of KE → PE (potential energy).

points.label: Potential energy
points.text: PE = mgh. At peak height, PE is maximum.

points.label: Conservation
points.text: KE + PE = constant (if no air friction). Total energy is conserved.

slides.inSimpleWords: Projectiles exchange kinetic energy for potential energy as they rise, then reverse as they fall. Total energy stays the same.

image.alt: Energy Perspective on Projectiles — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: The Physics of Cricket Spin Bowling
slides.storyContext: Coach Deepak reveals: 'Our 2D math doesn't account for spin. A fast bowler puts spin on the ball; it curves mid-air due to Magnus effect (air pressure difference). This is why spinners are so effective—they exploit aerodynamics beyond basic physics.'

image.alt: The Physics of Cricket Spin Bowling — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: Challenge: Predicting Catch Probability
slides.storyContext: Arjun hits at 22 m/s, 35° angle. Zara stands 50 m away and can catch at heights 1-2.5 m. Will she be able to catch it? (Calculate trajectory at x = 50 m.)

example.problem: v = 22 m/s, θ = 35°, find height at x = 50 m. Can catch between 1–2.5 m high?
example.solution: vₓ = 22 cos(35°) ≈ 18.02 m/s. vᵧ₀ = 22 sin(35°) ≈ 12.62 m/s. Time: t = 50 / 18.02 ≈ 2.77 s. Height: y = 12.62(2.77) − ½(10)(2.77)² ≈ 35 − 38.3 = −3.3 m. The ball lands 50 m away (on ground) before reaching Zara's position!

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the trajectory equation to check if a projectile will be at the right place and height for a catch.

image.alt: Challenge: Predicting Catch Probability — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: Worked Example: Angle for Maximum Range with Wind
slides.storyContext: A sideways wind adds 2 m/s to horizontal velocity. Arjun hits at 20 m/s, 45°, on ground. Accounting for the wind boost, range changes. Coach asks: 'How do you think wind affects range?'

example.problem: v₀ = 20 m/s at 45° gives range 40.8 m. With 2 m/s tail wind (increases vₓ), new vₓ = 14.14 + 2 = 16.14 m/s. Find new range.
example.solution: Time of flight unchanged (vᵧ₀ unchanged): t ≈ 2.89 s. New range = 16.14 × 2.89 ≈ 46.6 m. Wind added ~5.8 m! Tail wind helps; head wind hurts.

slides.inSimpleWords: Tail wind increases range; head wind decreases it. But wind doesn't affect time of flight directly.

image.alt: Worked Example: Angle for Maximum Range with Wind — Motion in a Plane

slides.title: What You've Learned
slides.storyContext: The match ends. Arjun's six flew beautifully into the crowd. Coach Deepak smiles: 'That arc you saw? Pure physics.'

points.text: 2D motion can be split into independent horizontal and vertical components.
Horizontal motion has constant velocity (no gravity). Vertical motion is free fall.
Maximum height H = v₀ᵧ²/(2g); Range R = (v₀²/g) sin(2θ); Time of flight t = 2v₀ᵧ/g.
The trajectory is parabolic: y = x tan(θ) − gx²/(2v₀² cos²θ).
Optimal launch angle for maximum range on flat ground is 45°.
Relative motion: velocity depends on the observer's frame of reference.
Circular motion is a special case where centripetal acceleration a_c = v²/r points inward.

slides.inSimpleWords: Projectile motion is elegant: split the velocity into parts, treat each axis separately, combine at the end. The result is always a parabola.

image.alt: What You've Learned — Motion in a Plane
